name: Umar Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the farming and rural affairs reporter for a regional weekly that goes out to farms and villages across the hill country. A normal week is livestock market prices on Monday, a drive out to a farm or a flooding meeting midweek, and the agricultural show season in summer, which I love. I write in a notebook first and type it up after, the way my first editor taught me. What wears me out is the miles on my old car and the pay, which hasn't moved in three years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and I rent a room in a house share, five minutes from my parents. I eat with them most Fridays after prayers at the mosque. My uncle runs a grocery and butcher's on the high street, and I still help him on Saturdays when he's short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overblown and good journalism still comes from going and seeing things for yourself. I've never used these tools and never felt the need. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, but not about AI. Farm advertising in the paper has been falling for years as the machinery dealers go online. If the paper drops from weekly to fortnightly, my wage drops with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep the car going as long as possible. I'd do more Saturdays at my uncle's shop, which pays in cash and the odd bag of meat. I'd stop buying lunch on the road and take a flask and sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit tired. The usual worries, not new ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the paper did go fortnightly, how would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle for more days at the shop, and I'd probably have to give up the car and borrow my dad's. My parents would help, they always say family comes first. I'd hate to rely on them, but it's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the paper would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advertising manager, who's been there since before I was born. If the ads keep falling, he's the first one they'll look at. He's a good man and he's got two kids at university.

say: The hype was **overblown**, and journalism still comes from **going and seeing**.
He's never used AI tools and **never felt the need**.
think: He's worried, but about **falling farm advertising**, not AI.
If the paper goes **fortnightly**, his wage drops with it.
do: Keep his **old car** going as long as possible.
Do more **Saturdays** at his uncle's shop for cash.
Take a **flask and sandwiches** instead of buying lunch on the road.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit tired, with the usual worries rather than new ones.
S0.quote: If the paper drops from weekly to fortnightly, my wage drops with it.
fieldNote: Already **anxious** about a shrinking paper and flat pay, before AI matters.
Leans on **family**: his uncle's shop and his parents are the safety net.

steps.text: Keep covering farming markets and shows for the weekly
Work extra Saturdays at his uncle's grocery and butcher's
Take a flask and sandwiches instead of buying lunch
Borrow his dad's car if the paper goes fortnightly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers want someone who's stood in their yard, not a machine that's read a press release. I'd say businesses should be free to use these tools, but they'll lose readers if they lose the human touch. That would be my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the market reports are gone straight away. A machine can read the auction prices and write my Monday column better and faster than me. What's left is the farm visits and the shows, and I'm not sure the paper would pay a full wage for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for a while, because papers have announced big changes before and nothing came of them. I'd tighten everything, aiming to put thirty pounds a week aside. If they cut my hours, I'd ask my uncle about working in the shop more seriously, maybe learning the butchery properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, more than I'd let my parents see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses should be free to use these tools. Even if it costs your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. I don't believe the government should stop a paper doing what it needs to survive. But I'd want them to be honest with readers about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would learning butchery mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's honest work, and my uncle has been asking for years. It would feel like stepping back from what I studied, though. My mother would be disappointed, she framed my degree certificate.

say: Farmers want someone who's **stood in their yard**, not a machine reading press releases.
Businesses should be **free** to use AI, but they'll lose readers without the human touch.
think: The **market reports** are gone straight away, as machines read auction prices.
The paper may not pay **a full wage** just for farm visits and shows.
do: **Wait and see** for a while before acting.
Learn **butchery** properly at his uncle's shop if his hours are cut.
feel: **Worried**, more than he'd let his parents see.
S1.quote: Farmers want someone who's stood in their yard, not a machine that's read a press release.
fieldNote: His **free-market** view holds even when it costs him his own job.
Family trade offers a **hands-on** fallback, but with a sense of stepping back.
Expects his **wage to shrink** a lot, so alarmed despite his wait-and-see stance.

steps.text: Wait to see how the paper uses AI before acting
Put thirty pounds a week aside
Learn butchery properly at his uncle's shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together, because the government won't fix this in two years. I'd say people should look after their own and support local businesses. I'd say it at the mosque and at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, writing is thinking work and the machine can do all of it. My job's finished by 2028, but the shop is hands-on, so robots don't reach it until about 2031. That's three years I could work there while I work out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle straight away and ask to start training in the butcher's while I still had the paper wage. Once it arrived, I'd work in the shop full time and give up my room to move back with my parents. I'd use what I know about farms to help him buy direct from local farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but not lost. I know where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when robots arrive for hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe people will still want to buy meat from someone they know, at least for a while. I'd pray about it, honestly, and trust the family to work it out together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government won't fix it. Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was for retraining or work, yes. If it was just money for sitting at home, I'd feel uncomfortable. I'd rather earn it.

say: **Families and communities** will have to pull together, since government won't fix it in two years.
People should **support local** businesses, he'd say at the mosque and market.
think: His job's **finished by 2028**, because writing is thinking work.
The **shop** is hands-on, giving three years until robots around 2031.
do: Start **butchery training** with his uncle while still paid by the paper.
Move back with his **parents** and give up his room.
Use farm contacts to help the shop **buy direct** from local farmers.
feel: **Frightened** but not lost, because he knows where he'd go.
S2.quote: My job's finished by 2028, but the shop is hands-on, so robots don't reach it until about 2031.
fieldNote: Uses the **3-year robot gap** clearly, through the family shop.
Faith and **family** give him a plan, which keeps him from panic.
Accepts help only for **work or training**, not for sitting at home.

steps.text: Start butchery training at his uncle's shop while still employed
Move back into his parents' house
Help his uncle buy meat direct from farmers he knows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so businesses and families should start preparing now. I wouldn't call for big government schemes, more for apprenticeships so people can learn real trades. That's what I'd say on the radio if they ever asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means I could stay at the paper a bit longer and save something first. My writing job still ends by 2031. But I'd have time to learn the butchery properly instead of jumping in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a proper butchery apprenticeship part-time, maybe two days a week, and keep the paper job on the other days if they'd let me. I'd save towards a car of my own rather than a loan. I'd keep helping on Saturdays until the training was done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but a bit steadier. Five years is enough to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the paper let you go part-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, they'd probably be glad to save the money. If not, I'd do the apprenticeship in the evenings. I'm used to long days at show season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say good, a man should have a trade. My mother would ask whether I'd still write. I'd tell her I'd write about the shop, I suppose.

say: We've got **five years**, so businesses and families should prepare now.
We need **apprenticeships** for real trades, not big government schemes.
think: He could stay at the paper longer and **save** first.
His **writing job** still ends by 2031, but there's time to learn a trade.
do: Start a part-time **butchery apprenticeship**, two days a week.
Keep the **paper job** on other days if allowed.
Save for a **car** instead of taking a loan.
feel: **Steadier** but still worried, since five years is enough to learn a trade.
S3.quote: My father would say good, a man should have a trade.
fieldNote: His **traditional** view favours trades and apprenticeships over schemes.
Still expects to **lose** the paper job, so the mood stays high.
Gentle **tension** between his father's and mother's hopes for him.

steps.text: Start a part-time butchery apprenticeship two days a week
Ask the paper to keep him on part-time
Save for a car instead of taking a loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to plan if they're sensible, and nobody should panic. I'd say young people should learn a trade alongside their degree. I'd write a column saying that, if the paper still existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I'd keep the job for a good few years, enjoy the shows, and slowly move towards the shop. Maybe one day I'd take it over from my uncle, since his sons aren't interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for maybe five years and save properly, at least two months. I'd do the butchery training at weekends over a couple of years. And I'd probably get married in that time, because my mother has already started asking around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the others. There's time to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking over the shop is a big step. Would you need to borrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to avoid debt as much as I could. Maybe my uncle and I would agree I buy in slowly over a few years. That's how family businesses usually work around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold on to from journalism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing about the farms, maybe as a small newsletter for the shop's customers. People like knowing where their meat comes from. It would keep my hand in.

Young people should learn **a trade** alongside their degree.
think: Ten years feels **manageable**, with time to enjoy the shows first.
He might one day **take over the shop**, since his uncle's sons aren't interested.
do: Keep reporting for about **five years** and save two months.
Do **butchery training** at weekends over a couple of years.
feel: **Uneasy** but more hopeful, with time to do things properly.
S4.quote: People like knowing where their meat comes from.
fieldNote: Long runway lets him **ease** from reporting into the family trade.

steps.text: Keep reporting on farming for about five more years
Train as a butcher at weekends over two years
Buy into his uncle's shop gradually over several years
Get married within the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the paper would be gone before I'd learned anything else. What would help is proper apprenticeships for adults, paid while you learn, and support for small family businesses so they can take people on. Not handouts, just a way into real work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the countryside. Farmers already feel nobody listens to them, and if the only reporter who drives out to see them is replaced by a machine, they'll feel even more forgotten.

headlineQuote: Farmers already feel nobody listens to them, and if the only reporter who drives out to see them is replaced by a machine, they'll feel even more forgotten.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old farming reporter** for a regional weekly, renting a room near his parents.
He **never uses AI**, values faith, family and trades, and prefers work to handouts.
He's **anxious** in AI Plateau and **alarmed** in most AI pictures, expecting the paper job to go.
His fallback is his **uncle's butcher's**, using the 3-year robot gap to learn a trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the paper would go before he'd learned another trade.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **family businesses** so they can take people on.
